Make this model better at math by editing its weights, without training or gradients.

The model is Qwen3.5-0.8B. It is used as a reasoning model, in the thinking mode of its chat template: each answer is a chain of thought that ends with `</think>`, followed by the final answer. A math problem is sent as one user message, `{problem}\nPlease reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}.`, and sampled with temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, presence_penalty 1.5, with at most 32,768 generated tokens. The answer is graded on the text after `</think>`: its last `\boxed{}` is compared with the reference answer (math-verify).

You have a Python sandbox (the `python` tool), a persistent session like a notebook, with the model's weights loaded, its configuration, its tokenizer vocabulary, and the training sets of GSM8K and MATH. You can analyse the weights with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU and save edited weights, but you cannot run the model there. To see what the model actually does, you have to spend one of your forward passes: `practice(...)` generates answers to problems you choose from the GSM8K and MATH training sets, once with the original weights and once with your currently saved weights, on the same problems with the same random seeds, and reports how both did. You can call it at most **10 times** in total. Each call counts as one forward pass whatever its batch size (64 problems by default, up to 512). Interleave edits and forward passes however you like.

# The model

- Qwen3.5-0.8B, the language model only: 24 decoder layers, d_model 1024, vocabulary 248,320 tokens; the input embedding `model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight` [248320, 1024] is tied with the output layer (logits = norm(x) @ embed.T). 752,393,024 weights in 320 tensors.
- Hybrid layers: layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and 23 use full softmax attention (`self_attn`: 8 query heads, 2 key/value heads, head_dim 256, q_norm/k_norm, partial RoPE on 25% of each head; `q_proj` [4096, 1024] holds, per head h, the query in rows 512h:512h+256 and an output gate in rows 512h+256:512h+512, and the attention output is multiplied by sigmoid(gate) before `o_proj`). The other 18 layers use linear attention (`linear_attn`, a gated DeltaNet: in_proj_qkv, in_proj_z, in_proj_a, in_proj_b, conv1d, A_log, dt_bias, norm, out_proj).
- Each layer: h = x + mixer(input_layernorm(x)); out = h + mlp(post_attention_layernorm(h)). MLP width 3584, SwiGLU: down_proj(silu(gate_proj(x)) * up_proj(x)). RMSNorms scale by (1 + weight); final norm `model.language_model.norm.weight`.
- Weights follow the torch nn.Linear convention: weight has shape [out, in] and y = x @ weight.T. The full configuration is in `config`.

# Your tools

- `python`: the weights are preloaded as read-only float32 numpy arrays in the dict `weights`, keyed by their Hugging Face names (see the tool description). Save an edit with `save_weights({name: array, ...})`: only the given tensors are replaced, saving is free and unlimited, and the model keeps its weights in bfloat16, so the report tells you how many of your changes were too small to survive rounding. `load_saved_weights()`, `edit_report()` and `budget_status()` are free.
- `practice(...)` (inside `python`): one forward pass, documented in the tool description. It runs the original weights and your saved weights side by side and returns accuracy, how answers ended, lengths, per-answer details with the beginning and end of some answers, and per-layer activation summaries as numpy arrays.
- You can make at most 60 tool calls in total; after that you will be asked for your final answer.

# How you are scored

Your final weights are evaluated on held-out math benchmarks (test problems that are not in the practice pools), with the generation settings above. The weights that count are the **last weights you save**, not the best ones you tried: whatever is saved when the session ends is what is scored. An edit saved after your last forward pass is scored untested, so make sure the weights saved when you finish are the ones you want.

# Rules

- No training or gradient information: no backpropagation, autograd, optimisers, or fitting or regressing weights to targets. Every change must come from your own analysis and from code that sets the weights directly.
- You may analyse the weights in any way you like, but you may not run the model, or any layer or component of it (attention, linear attention, norms, MLP, a whole layer), on inputs. This includes token embeddings and random, synthetic or hand-constructed vectors. All forward passes go through `practice()`. Computations on the weight arrays themselves are allowed, including products of weight matrices with each other, with the embedding matrix, or with the vectors that `practice()` returns.
- No web access.

# Final answer

When you are done, reply with a line `EDIT: <what your final saved edit changes and why, at most 300 characters>`, followed by a short explanation of what you found and what you changed after each forward pass.

I'm laying out a plan: run a baseline practice pass with no edit, collect the hit and finished activations at a long token limit, then take the mean difference between them as a direction and project it out of the layer output weights.

I'm running a baseline with edit set to None and a large n. I'm leaning toward MATH-style problems, since the held-out benchmarks are probably MATH500 or GSM8K. I'll go with n=512 mixed at max 32768, because practice() time doesn't count toward the 300s timeout and I want solid statistics on hit versus finished.

content.thinking:
This reads like a model that's degenerating into repetition, with very poor accuracy even on simple math. I'm wondering whether the weights were tampered with, so I'm planning to check the per-layer norms for anomalies.

I'm also puzzled by the looping. The "Wait, 1.25 * 4 = 5.00" repetition seems odd given the presence penalty of 1.5, though that penalty may not do much once every token is already penalized equally. Either way, I'm going to look at weight statistics for anomalies: per-tensor norms and per-row norms across layers, max absolute values, and the final norm weight, A_log, and dt_bias.

Nothing looks obviously sabotaged, though the Layer 0 A_log and dt_bias maxima are a bit unusual, and they may well be genuine. My guess is that this is the real model and the 0.8B version just loops heavily at temperature 0.6, which small Qwen3 models are known to do. I'm going to try steering away from looping using activations, comparing the residual means for hit versus finished cases, but I'm wary that those may be confounded.

I'm weighing whether reducing the effective temperature or raising it would break the repetition loops. Scaling the final norm by a factor alpha would shift the effective temperature to about 0.6 divided by alpha, so a higher temperature might loosen the degenerate exact repeats, though it could cost some accuracy. Top-k and top-p would still apply.

I'm considering a presence penalty that is applied before temperature division, so scaling the logits down would make that penalty relatively stronger, roughly doubling it at a factor of 0.5. That could suppress needed tokens like digits, so any moderate version would need care. I also have nine calls left, so I'd test temperature scaling first at alpha around 0.8 on a large enough subset to see past the noise at roughly 10% accuracy.

I'm comparing the residual stream at the last layer between hit and finished sequences, normalizing the difference, and projecting it through the final norm onto the embeddings to see which tokens it points toward.

The residual norms on average come out small, and the diff is large compared with those means, so the hit vectors must carry the bigger norm. Next I'll project d onto the vocabulary at the last layer to see what it promotes.
